text_fidelity_a:
Amazon Kindle Fire HD 8.9" Standing Leather Case, Fuchsia (will not fit HDX models) This case fits very well and was designed specifically for the Kindle Fire HD 8.9"—with even slick cutouts for the speakers in the back. The Fire just pops right into it and it couldn't be neater or slimmer. The magnetic closure is tidy and holds the case closed quite well. I think Amazon must be trying to recoup some from its bargain-level pricing of its Kindles, however, because I think it's over-priced for what it is (at least at the time of this writing). Still, you can't beat the fit of it.

But a caution is in order for the leather lovers: This may be "genuine leather" but it sure doesn't look or feel like it. If you get it in black or the Saddle Tan, maybe, but the one I was given to review (fuschia) just looks like fancy plastic to me. It has a pebbly texture that makes it easy to hold, but if you want that rich, satisfying feel of well-worn wallet leather, you won't get it with this case. (The Verso Prologue cases have that feel.)

As with so many of the Kindle cases on the market, the inability to clip a stylus to the case is I think an omission. I have a rooCase for my Kindle Fire 7" that I like specifically because I can clip my stylus to the pocket that holds the Kindle. Maybe some hot new designer will come up with a way to design a very slim case that can stow a stylus.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Kindle Fire HD 8.9" Standing Leather Case, Fuchsia (will not fit HDX models)

text_fidelity_a:
Srhythm NC35 Noise Cancelling Headphones Wireless Bluetooth 5.0, Fast Charge Over-Ear Lightweight Headset with Microphones,Mega Bass 50+ Hours’ Playtime I want to point out up front, for those who are afraid these will be too big for a small head, that they fit me fine. I have a small head. I am a short woman, I have little ears, a little head. When these headphones are adjusted to be fully contracted, even without doing any bending of the top part, they fit great. They are lightweight but substantial, very comfortable, and I can see myself listening to them for hours without discomfort. I can lean back in my recliner without anything touching the headphones.

I didn’t know about the whole thing about burning in headphones. I’ve spent the last few hours down that rabbit hole, with all the opinions pro and con, etc., and I’m glad I’m doing it because I can already tell the headphones are responding to the burn-in process. I went to Spotify and looked for burn-in playlists, and I’m playing through one of them now.

I will not use these for noise cancelling, so I cannot comment on that. I want headphones that don’t bother my ears during hours of listening, that give me a clean, clear experience of the dynamics of the music, and that seem to become a part of me. So far, these are doing that. When I first started listening, I could tell these headphones were a little stiff and muddy, but they are loosening up now and becoming quite wonderful. I’m very pleased. And I’m only a few hours into the burning in.

Update: I just tried the ANC button. I’m sitting here, still in burn-in, watching the news on TV and periodically checking in to be sure the burn-in playlist is still playing. I could hear the TV when I was listening to Alice in Chains, and then I turned on the noise cancelling/ANC switch. Hey, this noise cancelling works pretty good! Of course, you get more pressure in your ears with ANC turned on, so it’s not a mode I would listen in for very long, but it definitely cancels the noise. Can’t hear a thing from the TV now. Flip the ANC switch, and I hear the TV. Flip it again, and there’s no voices coming through from the TV.
text_fidelity_b: Srhythm NC35 Noise Cancelling Headphones Wireless Bluetooth 5.0, Fast Charge Over-Ear Lightweight Headset with Microphones,Mega Bass 50+ Hours’ Playtime

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin Nuvi 2595LMT UPDATE: after installing the latest map update and waiting for a very long time for the install software to do its thing and worrying if it had actually finished the install because after about an hour my computer said "the application has unexpectedly quit," the device seems to be working perfectly.

Overall, I like the 2595LMT. It boots and finds the satellites faster and has more information available.

Pros:
1. I can press the lower left "Arrive time" button and change it to a variety of readouts: miles remaining, altitude, time via.
2. Voice command works, mostly, especially on simple commands like "Go Home." More complex commands, like an address, return a wide variety of responses, most of them wrong. (Why it's searching the entire United States when it knows where I am and should be looking locally is beyond me.) I liked the old way of narrowing search to State, then City, then Address. Now it just asks you for the whole address, which it likely doesn't understand.
3. It's slimmer and lighter.
4. Easy to import my favorites from my old Nuvi into the 2595LMT. Using a PC, after plugging the old Nuvi into a computer using the USB port,

a. Navigate until you find the "current.GPX" file on the old Nuvi and
b. Copy it to your desktop (this is also a way to make a backup should you desire.)
c. Rename the file: replace "current" with any word you want, as long as it's not "current") so that it is names "anyword.gpx"
d. Attach the new Nuvi 2595LMT to the computer and navigate until you find the folder with its "current.gpx" file.
e. Copy the "anyword.gpx" file from the desktop into the same folder where the "Current.gpx" file resides.
f. Disconnect and restart. All the old favorites will be added to the current list in your new Nuvi.

5. It doesn't say "recalculating" when you disregard its directions
6. It has lane indicators: a series of arrows in the upper left that tell you which lane to get into to make the next turn. Very cool.
7. Touch screen allows scrolling like a smartphone, at least on some screens.
8. Allows you to add/edit shortcuts like a PC. You can create and move icons around so that you can get to a particular feature with one touch.
9. Micro-SD card only
10. Bigger screen
11. 3-D view of the road
12. Speed limit indicator and simultaneous readout of your actual speed that turns red if you exceed the local speed limit. (I wish it bonged quietly when the speed limit changed to remind you that you have to go slower or can go faster.)

Cons:
1. Sadly, on my unit (even after map and software updates) when I say, "Find Place" it immediately crashes and reboots. And if I say, "Find City" it ignores me, even if I ask it to find New York or Los Angeles. I may try reinstalling the software in case it loaded incompletely for some reason. (UPDATE: I waited a couple of weeks and tried updating the maps again. This time it fully installed and happily all the voice commands now work very well. This alone is a good reason to get is unit. Typing while driving is difficult and dangerous. Voice command is simply wonderful and something I've always wanted in a Garmin.)
2. Stuff has been moved around so that the interface is a bit foreign. For instance, "Favorites" are now "Saved Places" and trying to save or edit a saved place is confusing until you get the hang of it.
3. Doesn't have a powered cradle anymore, only a standard mini-USB on the back. Not a real problem, but it's slower to hook up and remove. I used to be able to drop it on the cradle and go. Now I have to find the end of the cable and thread it into a small port on the back. Minor.
4. The traffic function in my opinion is a joke. Driving LA freeways at most times involves congestion and some delay. It's simply the way it is. The Garmin hates congestion and is constantly trying to get you around it. Thus it's constantly bonging and telling me to get off the freeway to take surface streets, assuming they are magically uncongested when in reality the surface streets during rush hour are ten times worse. I'm pretty much going to ignore its traffic suggestions and may turn it off altogether. If you buy the amazon basics power cord [[ASIN:B003N2POXK AmazonBasics Vehicle Power Cable with Mini-USB Connector for GPS and Other Mini-USB Devices]] it doesn't have a built in traffic receiver and thus defeats the annoying and constant attempts to route you around congestion. Simply put, don't believe the alternate route is going to save you any time. Getting onto surface streets during rush hour is a recipe for even longer delays.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin Nuvi 2595LMT

for New Solis Lite Listing, go to: https://www.Amazon.com/dp/B08YKB6VMN?ref=myi_Title_dp I love this thing! I only returned it because I didn’t get it in time for my travel and searched high and low for any local stores to sell them and I found 1! Prices were pretty much the same everywhere online.

I went through my carrier, Verizon and sure you can get a jet pack or some mobile WiFi device but you still have to pay monthly charges (like a mobile phone) which isn’t worth it for me. I don’t travel often so I don’t want to pay for something I won’t be using.

This device is awesome! You don’t need a SIM card which seemed like a requirement for other mobile WiFi devices during my search. They have many plans you can choose from or pay as you go. It’s wireless and charged fully quickly. You can track your usage and purchase more data (if you’re not on an unlimited plan). Once you’ve used up data, you’re cut off so there’s no surprise overage costs.

The app for me wasn’t as user friendly but support was available right away via app. I they believed there was a glitch with mine. The remaining data kept changing (significantly) at first. After resetting it, seemed to fix the problem.

I didn’t see an option to have users enter password every time. My kids set their devices to auto connect so they would connect without knowing (if I didn’t check usage). This drained my data. The other negative thing I would say is that it tells you how many devices are connected but not who or what is connected unless I just didn’t see the option (again, not user friendly to me). All this is minor given my research on what was available.

Why didn’t I use my Verizon hot spot? I wanted to make sure I was able to connect without issues and upload/download without issues. My experiences with the 4g hot spot was terrible. The 5G isn’t as bad (but I didn’t know that since I had just upgraded my phone).
text_fidelity_b: for New Solis Lite Listing, go to: https://www.Amazon.com/dp/B08YKB6VMN?ref=myi_Title_dp

Western Digital 320GB WD Black Performance Mobile Hard Drive - 7200 RPM Class, SATA 6 Gb/s, , 32 MB Cache, 2.5" - WD3200LPLX Update 8-7-19: I went to the WD website to register my two drives. They show as no warranty from WD, presumably because they were bought through a reseller. Just so you know ...

I use these as primary storage (and backup storage) for our MacBook Air laptop. Most MacBooks now come with solid state drives, meaning memory chip based drives, not physical spinning disks. They are much more expensive than the heritage physical disk approach, such that the largest SSD that we could get with our 2017 MacBook Air was a 256 GB drive. These WD Black (virtually enterprise level) drives are 500 GB each, so our storage is 2x that of the built in drive. We use one as our primary external drive; once a month we install the 2nd drive (also externally), copy the files across, and put it into our safe deposit box at the bank. If we ever lose a drive, whether to failure or someone breaking in and stealing our drive and laptop, we're only 30 days behind, a real advantage.

The only downside to this drive is that the warranty on the drive itself is provided by the Seller, OEMGENUINE. The drive came marked with a label on the drive as a Seller 5 year warranty, with no terms provided. The downside risk is there is no published warranty, either by the Seller or by WD on their website, and whatever warranty is provided is subject to the Seller still being in existence over the next 5 years. However, given the price of the drive ($35 or so), it was a reasonable risk to take, especially since we acquired two and use one as the backup to the primary one. The odds of losing two drives at the same time is pretty remote. So we accepted the risk, but dropped the review for the product & seller by 1 star. If you go to the WD website, they do claim a 5 year limited warranty. I am a little surprised that the WD website doesn't provide a link to their warranty. So if we can't reach OEMGENUINE should we have a problem, I'm not sure what protection we'll have from WD. Something to consider if that's important to you.

These are fast drives (7200 rpm for the 500GB drive), which is noticeably faster than the previous bulk drives we've purchased online and/or removed from existing systems, which have all been 5400 rpm drives. SATA compatible, plug and play, no issues yet but it's only been a few days. If something materially changes, I'll post an update.
text_fidelity_b: Western Digital 320GB WD Black Performance Mobile Hard Drive - 7200 RPM Class, SATA 6 Gb/s, , 32 MB Cache, 2.5" - WD3200LPLX

Sennheiser Momentum Headphone - Brown I am so very pleased with these headphones. I was expecting them to sound pretty good given the Sennheiser lineage, but they really set me back on my heels with the sound quality, comfort, and overall design.

Let's start with the easy one - how they look. To my eye, they are very nicely styled. Classic-looking rather than flashy. I especially like how the headband is not excessively padded -- it does not stick out when you wear them. Very elegant overall. Everything looks and feels high quality.

They also hit the mark regarding comfort. I usually have a 1 hour limit when it comes to over-the-ear headphones, in that after an hour of wearing them I've reached my limit of tolerance. These, however, felt wonderful. They are light enough that I hardly noticed the weight. More importantly, the ear cups fit me just right. Cushy enough to seal out ambient noise but not at the expense of having my ears feel like they were trapped in a vice. They felt just as good well into hour 2 as they did in the first 15 minutes. I found the headband also very comfortable for long stretches without getting "sweaty head" as I get with other headphones.

But it's the sound that counts. To my ear, these `phones deliver in spades. I started off with some Stanley Clarke. Wonderful -- ample bass but not at the expense of hearing every string being plucked. I listened to School Days a couple of times in a row, just amazed at how good it sounded. The same for Florence and the Machine -- solid, deep bass but not overwhelming.

Next up was Metric to see how vocals come through. Again, superb. I was finally able to figure out some of the lyrics on Synthetica that never came through clear enough on my ear buds. Regina Spektor was also an absolute pleasure to listen to and have all facets of her unique vocal styling come through so clearly.

I also tried them for movie watching on my Fire, and again was very pleased. Dialog was clean and pronounced; explosions were, well, explosive.

The noise isolation is quite good. These are not noise cancelling headphones, so some ambient noise will leak in, but it keeps out everything other than the most significant ambient sounds.

I really can't fault these on any criterion. They look great, feel great, and sound great. Granted, the price is not so great, but good quality costs. If you're a demanding headphone user, these are worth the money charged. Highly recommend.
text_fidelity_b: Sennheiser Momentum Headphone - Brown

Surge Protector Power Strip with USB, Silicone Extension Cord with 10 Outlets 3 USB Charging Ports and 1 USB-C Charging Port, 1875W/15A Overload Surge Protection, Gift for Mother's Day PROS

1. It has 10 sockets/outlets.
2. Two of the sockets are offset from the other six. This allows them to be used for wide plugs, which is an important feature, because wide plugs are a frequent occurrence on appliances.
3. The color is an attractive but neutral black which makes the strip fade into the background more than the strips I own which are white or beige.
4. In addition to being a power strip, it also provides surge protection.
5. There are four USB ports that can be used for charging devices. One of them is a USB-C port and the other 3 are standard USB ports. The manufacturer claims in the manual that the three standard USB ports are “smart” USB ports.

CONS

1. I am not entirely comfortable trusting the “smart” USB ports on this device for charging. I feel more comfortable using a regular USB charging adapter and plugging it into a socket on the surge protector side of this device.

2. Regarding the smart USB ports, there are not adequate instructions either in the manual or on the manufacturer’s website that clearly explain the implications of this feature and how to utilize it. I cannot find information on the top mA it supports in charging.

GENERAL INFORMATION ON USB CHARGING

In order to test this device for my Vine review, I spent over two hours (!!!) trying to find comprehensible information on what the term “smart” means in the context of a USB port on a power strip like this one. Unfortunately, I was left with more questions than answers, for which hassle I’m dropping a star off this review. I’ve included some of what I learned below, for what it might be worth to any fellow Amazon customer who might be thinking of purchasing this product.

A smart USB charger port supposedly can, in and of itself, figure out what the optimal charging speed of a specific device is when it is plugged into that port, in order to neither overload it with too much current or under-deliver to it the optimal current. The question on everyone’s mind these days (it certainly has been on mine), is whether it is possible to destroy the battery in a particular device by slamming too much current into it. Apparently, the answer to this all-important question is: No. If, for example, you take a phone which comes with a 900mA wall charger, and you plug it into a 2,100mA charger that comes with a different device you own, it will not damage the phone. It will only speed up the length of time it takes for the phone’s battery to charge. However, if you have a USB device older than 2007, it may not charge on any USB ports newer than the (now ancient), 500mA USB 1.0 and 2.0 PC ports. Which means such older devices may not charge even on the “smart” USB ports on this device.

USB charging current is measured in mA (milliampere, 1/1000 of an ampere, the basic unit for measuring electrical current). There are three kinds of USB ports which are defined by their current specs: a standard downstream port, a charging downstream port, and a dedicated charging port. The first two are found on a desktop computer. The third kind is a “dumb” wall charger.

USB 1.0 and 2.0 standard downstream ports on a computer can deliver up to 500mA (0.5A).

USB 3.0 standard downstream ports on a computer can deliver up to 900mA (0.9A).

USB 3.1 and USB 3.2 ports can deliver between 1,500mA (1.5A) and 3,000mA (3A).

Charging downstream USB ports on a computer can deliver up to 1,500mA (1.5A).

Dedicated USB charging ports on a computer can deliver up to 3,000mA (3A).
text_fidelity_b: Surge Protector Power Strip with USB, Silicone Extension Cord with 10 Outlets 3 USB Charging Ports and 1 USB-C Charging Port, 1875W/15A Overload Surge Protection, Gift for Mother's Day

After all the initial problems and concerns I have had it installed and working for about a month I guess. It's working great on a variety of different software and protocols. I even tried connecting it to the Angelcam website and using DDNS. Works great with just about everything. With the 128GB SD card it does great. I uploaded some new photos of it working and the different clients being used securely. This turned out to be a great buy because the image quality is incredible and it's got an incredibly wide angle.

You cannot see the IR light like that at night it's only because of the camera I used you can see it. I did that for a reason so that everyone could see the amount of IR light it puts out. BEFORE EDIT AND CUSTOMER SUPPORT:

After that you will find several screws lowered besides the lens and IR area. You only need to remove the 4 of the screws. Underneath the lens is the board that holds the SD-Card. Their support was nice enough to send me a video later on. I plan on posting that later after I get this all working. As of now it is telling me I need to reset the camera and there is no reset button that I can find. In my opinion this is very poorly designed and not very good for people who like to customize or configure their devices. I do not like the way the it acts as soon as it connects to your network. More to come on this product but for now I do not recommend buying this unless you are familiar with IP camera installation, network configuration, and have some electrical experience as far as handling circuit boards. text_fidelity_a:
Philips DVT5000/00 4 GB Digital Voice Tracer with 3 Built-in Microphones Voice Recorder This is a good voice recorder. Whether you need it to record your voice memos, lectures, meetings, or discretely record your favorite spy, this will surely be a recorder you'll find many uses for.

It feels very secure in your hand, and has a comfortable feel and weight. It comes with a small pouch, which is nice. The record button is easy to find my sight or feel. The volume and forward/reverse buttons are on an outer button from the record button. Play and stop on the left and index and menu are on the right.

f1 and f2 buttons are primarily used for setting mic sensitivity and voice quality. Under Mic Sensitivity you can choose: Dictate (good for personal memos), Speech recognition (turns on when it hears voice), conversation (good for interviews or conversations, auto zoom (good for large areas where there may be close up voices and far voices), and lecture (good for lectures)

You can choose either low quality at 8kbps in Mp3 format to super high quality 192kbps in mp3. There is also a wave format in 1411 kbps. The higher quality you go impacts total record time. You can add a micro SD card for adding recording time.

There are also 4 index folders labeled A thru D. These are for separating projects. There is also a folder you could place music files if you wanted this to be a mp3 player.

There is also a menu setting where the voice quality and mic sensitivity can be accessed as well as numerous other options such as splitting files, display contrast, and clearvoice (an option that improves the sound quality of the recorded voiec)

The unit comes with rechargable AA batteries that will need to be charged when you first open it. They charge with the included usb to micro USB cord. Any other micro USB cord you own will also work. Once the recorder is connected to your computer through the USB cable you can download and upload voice or mp3 and wave files.

The only thing I wish this had was different settings for each index. For instance I would have liked to set index A for lecture mode at high quality, index B for dictate at a lower quality, etc. Once you set a mic sensitivity and recording quality, they are the same for all index until you change them in settings.

Overall a great quality recorder. Great for meetings, memos, and conversations.
text_fidelity_b: Philips DVT5000/00 4 GB Digital Voice Tracer with 3 Built-in Microphones Voice Recorder

text_fidelity_a:
Ultimate Ears MEGABOOM 3 Portable Wireless Bluetooth Speaker (Powerful Sound + Thundering Bass, Bluetooth, Magic Button, Waterproof, Battery 20 hours) - Lagoon Blue I used to be a big Ultimate Ears guy from the aughts before they were bought by Logitech who killed their best product lines and replaced it with stuff like... THIS. The tiresome photos of impossibly gleeful adult-babies listening to music underwater and having the times of their lives thanks to this f——g speaker really gets cloying when it’s printed on literally everything except the device itself. But that’s Logitech for you. Of all things I have to complain about with this speaker, the sound isn’t one of them. Unlike its predecessors and smaller cousins, the Megaboom 3 doesn’t peak out the bass quite so much when it would otherwise be distorted. (This is the most common bit of digital audio gimmickry to fool you into think it sounds “crystal clear”.) The people complaining about this speaker in these reviews who say other brands are better are just brands more notorious for “loudness fakery” to make the sound seem more bass-heavy but is really just slick audio post-processing. It’s makes hip hop sound a little better but everything else is a murky mess. But I digress. This speaker does all of the digital trickery, sure, but at least the actual amplifier and speaker drivers aren’t rubbish so that’s I plus. I was playing System of a Down cranked in my bedroom and it sounded amazing, especially compared to my former Boom speaker which someone nicked from my garage. Where the Boo crumpled trying to product screeching highs and thumping lows the Megaboom 3 dominated. Of course I don’t use any of the EQ tomfoolery and let it play as close to how the music was engineered to play and its just dandy. Okay then, good sound: check.
The problem with this speaker, like all of the other UE speakers, is the brain-dead user interface and obnoxious audio feedback that you can’t properly adjust without hacking the device configs (allegedly). There is literally a single on/off switch for all audio feedback. Wut? No relative volume of system sounds compared to music, or selection of which sounds you want to hear and which ones you don’t, like that HORRIBLY OBNOXIOUS LOUD BEEP it makes that’s louder than the music if you accidentally lean in on your volume up button? Of course every sound is as loud as or louder than the music your playing. That’s just great. Furthermore, if you are listening to music through your iPad or iPhone, it decides to insert little beeps for certain feedback notifications that never happen when you are just using your device without the speaker. It’s horribly distracting and unnecessary, but worse is that you NEED audio feedback on if you want to be able to Bluetooth connect to it as audio feedback is the only feedback you get.

Ugh. Sorry, had a bit of a rant there.

It’s tough because I think the speak sounds decent and almost worth the price, but the UI team at Logite... excuse me... Ultimate Ears are clearly huffing paint fumes as each product they subsequently release is even more unpleasant to use than the last. Don’t let the coked-out looking teens with bright, expensive clothing printed on the box fool you.
text_fidelity_b: Ultimate Ears MEGABOOM 3 Portable Wireless Bluetooth Speaker (Powerful Sound + Thundering Bass, Bluetooth, Magic Button, Waterproof, Battery 20 hours) - Lagoon Blue

text_fidelity_a:
Sony HDR-PJ380/W High Definition Handycam Camcorder with 3.0-Inch LCD (White) (Discontinued by Manufacturer) While I'm quite comfortable using an SLR, I've not been all that handy with a camcorder in the past. It's been a few years since I used one, so I was curious to see if user-friendliness has kept pace with technological advancements.

With this model it has. I found it very easy to use right out of the box with just some minor trial and error. I did end up reading the manual (which is pretty decent) but the main functions were pretty self apparent by just fiddling around with it a bit. The menu structure is logical and well presented; the screen is clear and easy to view.

The overall build quality is excellent. It feels more substantial in hand than I expected at this price point while retaining a very lightweight and easy to carry profile. I like the button placement - feels very natural in hand.

I love having the internal memory for storage as well as the little touches, such as a built-in USB connector. These features help make this a grab-and-go type of device, which increases the likelihood and ease of bringing it along and capturing video. (Note: you can also use a plug-in memory card should you want to.)

The video quality in good light/outdoors is excellent - very sharp and clear. Low-light performance is a somewhat grainy but quite decent. Stills are pretty decent. It won't put an SLR to shame, but it's more than good enough for casual snapshots. The internal mic works well and is more immune to wind noise than I expected.

My only significant disappointment with the cam is the projector. Wonderful idea, but the actual performance is lackluster. The projected video is hard to see clearly if there's any appreciable amount of light in the room. The 100 inch projection spec is wildly optimistic if you expect to actually see what is being projected.

Given that this cam does everything else so well, is so easy to use, and a breeze to tote along, I won't detract any stars due to the shortcomings of the projector feature. This is a great cam for the novice cam user (such as myself) or even an intermediate user. However, if the projection feature is a primary need, this may not be a good cam for your needs.
text_fidelity_b: Sony HDR-PJ380/W High Definition Handycam Camcorder with 3.0-Inch LCD (White) (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

Epica Digital Emergency Solar Hand Crank AM/FM/NOAA Radio, Flashlight, Smartphone Charger with NOAA Certified Weather Alert & Cable-ONE Cable Does All This is one of those products that is good to have, but even better if you never need to use it since you'll probably be using it when the electricity is out. It offers a lot of functionality in a compact size: a flashlight, AM radio, FM radio and weather band radio. It runs off of an internal rechargeable battery that is kept charged either via solar power, USB connection or by cranking the handle. It can also serve as a source to charge a cell phone (albeit with very limited capacity to do so since the internal battery is only rated at 800mAh).

It works pretty well. The flashlight is very bright - had no problems lighting my way down a dark stairway and in a totally dark room. The radio is OK. The reception is spotty and it only picked up a few of the very strong stations in the area. It's very susceptible to positioning - moving it just a couple of inches turned a clear station into static.

Cranking the handle to keep it charged is pretty easy. It turns easily and the handle is comfortable. According to the manual, one minute of cranking equals 30 minutes of flashlight use or 20 minutes of radio use.

This is a good product to keep on hand in case of emergency, such as a bad storm or extended power outage. It won't keep you cool in the summer or warm in the winter, but at least you can see where you're going and listen to the radio. Definitely worth a spot in the emergency kit. The only shortcoming is the somewhat limited radio reception.
[sample provided by manufacturer for review]
text_fidelity_b: Epica Digital Emergency Solar Hand Crank AM/FM/NOAA Radio, Flashlight, Smartphone Charger with NOAA Certified Weather Alert & Cable-ONE Cable Does All

But, when I'm in need of some close up photography of something related to my hobbies (I share a lot), I want to take the best pictures possible. The Fositan light box is simple to stand up or take down. It stores easily, has a carrying strap and looks like a poster folio when folded. The LED lights are great, with a clean white light that is dimmable. There's a diffuser panel that goes inside and softens the light, eliminating reflections. It has three ports that are closed with velcro. One on top and two in the front. Each port cover can be completely removed or adjusted to your liking. The backdrop panels are nice, heavy matte sheets of plastic. With a good enough range of colors to suit just about any requirements. They are held in place by straps, one at the very front of the bottom and one at the very top of the back. And, of course, if you want, you can always make your own 'custom' backdrops out of nearly any sheet material that you can trim to fit. text_fidelity_a:
Onkyo HT-S3500 660 Watt 5.1-Channel Home Theater Speaker/Receiver Package This system ROCKS! We got it for our Roku, and aside from a few slight annoyances with the setup, it works and sounds awesome. It works very well for our living room and my wife can now hear the movies instead of asking me what they said all the time. I would like to point out for some people that the HDMI output to the TV is only for the HDMI inputs and not "One port to rule them all". If you use a component device with the red, blue and green plugs (us: older DVD player) you need to have a set run from component out to the component in on the TV. Same goes with the RCA style (red, yellow, white) to get video on that. I was very disappointed that I couldn't just run one HDMI to the TV and be done with it.

Secondly the unit gets warm. I mean very warm and electronic smelly. I read the other reviews and I also experienced a similar issue. So after a week, I grabbed an unused 120mm computer fan and a old router power supply and made a cooling fan that rests on the top of the head unit. It helped a ton. I no longer smell anything, and the whole thing is now cool to the tough. I control the power to the fan using one of those green power strips that turns off stuff. Others used a USB fan from the iPod port on the unit. I do recommend that you cool this somehow to increase its lifespan.

The speaker wire that came with the system is junk and too short for my purposes. I ordered some thicker gauge wire [[ASIN:B0029HHIDY RCA AH16100SN 100 Ft. 16-Gauge Speaker Wire]]for my needs. The sounds is great with this better/bigger wire and I could put it where I wanted.

So these maybe deal breakers for some, but the price was right and we live with the other issues, but since this unit works so well, it seems like a small price to pay for good sound. Overall I highly recommend this unit.
text_fidelity_b: Onkyo HT-S3500 660 Watt 5.1-Channel Home Theater Speaker/Receiver Package

WAVLINK USB 3.0 Universal Docking Station with DVI/HDMI Dual Monitor Docking Station,2 USB 2.0 Port,2 USB 3.0 Port,Gigabit Ethernet,Quick Charging,Supports for Windows Mac OS The links on their site for the software download were not working, so I ended up having to go directly to DisplayPort to download the update. After that it was pretty smooth sailing.

I have kiddo all hooked up with dual monitors and his laptop docked and stored. So, now he has actual room at his desk to put his notebook or textbook or whatever else he needs for school, without the laptop taking up half his space.

To avoid any latency issues you can sometimes get while gaming and using DisplayPort software, I did hook his main monitor up directly to his laptop and "mirrored" the screen. This is the one he will play his games on. For his second monitor used for videos, research, etc. I used the HDMI port on the Wavlink dock and "extended" the screen. This way he can have dual monitors and bypass any latency issues that sometimes can crop up. If you can, it is also recommend when gaming to plug the mouse directly into the laptop as well, rather than the dock.

Personally, I don't notice any latency issues on either monitor or when the mouse is hooked up through the dock. But it was easy enough to just bypass the issue all together by how I plugged stuff in. The only struggles I had were with setting up his laptop to not go into hibernate instead of sleep after 2 hours, to stop disabling power to USBs while in sleep, and to allow his keyboard to wake the system out of sleep even though it was clearly already set up to do so. But that is nothing to do with the dock, and everything to do with Windows 10 being a pain in the behind sometimes. Finally everything is all set up, behaving as it should and we are ready for school to start next week. Well I'm ready, him... not so much.
text_fidelity_b: WAVLINK USB 3.0 Universal Docking Station with DVI/HDMI Dual Monitor Docking Station,2 USB 2.0 Port,2 USB 3.0 Port,Gigabit Ethernet,Quick Charging,Supports for Windows Mac OS

It did take me a moment or two of fiddling to figure out how the case doubles as a stand. The table frame insert can also be completely detached to allow you to move the Nexus into portrait view when using the case as a stand.

The only miss is that I would have liked to have one of those stretchy elastic bands on the back so I could slip my hand through when holding it. But overall, I found this to be a good case and a good value for its price point.

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin nüvi 255W 4.3-Inch Portable GPS Navigator (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I bought this as a graduation present for my nephew and, of course, had to try it out for a while just to make sure it was "in proper functioning order." (OK, so I like toys even more than the kids do).

Very nice system! It's a nice improvement from earlier Nuvi's I've used. Love the improved software, especially the full-time next-turn indicator (long a favorite feature of mine on Magellan units). The screen layout is attractive and easy to use, even for those of us with less than perfect eyesight.

While I personally like the Magellan systems better for my own use, I picked this for the nephew for a couple of reasons. First, it has features such as the ability to download Google maps directions. Not something I would use, but a nice feature for those who would use it. Second, it has the ability to display the speed limit. While it won't prevent speeding, at least it's a reminder for a younger driver to keep it slow.

I found the routing engine to be top-notch. Every GPS does that a bit different, but every route I planned on it was plotted out in a logical manner. It's a bit slower to detect off-route conditions and re-route compared with Magellans, but certainly does it at an acceptable speed. Boot up and acquitiion time is very good, as it the overall build quality and form factor.

A good option to pick up is a bean bag mount such as a NavMat. Makes it far easier to hide the GPS without any trace to tip off potential theves.

Most important, it has Garmin support - they are far better than Magellan, and can be used as a resource for someone who is using their first GPS. I was sorry to have to hand it back over the the nephew, but he's thrilled with it!
text_fidelity_b: Garmin nüvi 255W 4.3-Inch Portable GPS Navigator (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a:
Symphonized Wired Earbuds with Microphone - Noise Isolating Headphones with Wire, Ear Buds with Wire, Headphones with Microphone for Computer, Corded Earbuds, Travel Headphones 3.5mm Graduation Gift Holy crap I like these! And I'm only on the 3rd of auditioning them! I got the red pair so they were only $21. Grab a pair and keep them as spares or give them to a friend who is listening to cheep buds.

No kidding while they may technically be 'better' I'd pick these to listen to over the ZR Carbon Tenor which were $40. I've been breaking in my Carbo Tenore for hours and hours and tip tuning to hope to like them move. This NRG are more musical and engaging. There is nice bass extension and bloom but there is still nice articulation. It's a bit much for me, but I'm buying them for someone who likes plenty of bass. The acoustic guitar sounds good, but not great (I play acoustic guitar). The carboTenore do a better job with an acoustic guitar, but there is nothing really wrong with how they handle the guitar.

They are not for people who like an upfront mid-range. Voices are a touched recessed. They lack a bit of chestiness in male vocals but not enough to be a fault (using Stevie Ray Vaughn to check). Just a sound signature thing. Female vocals sound good (using Annie Lennox to check)

While not much for soundstage there is some air around the instruments. They do an adequate job of capturing the room the instruments are played in. On both these counts, I like it more than on the Tenore. It's not a big difference but it's something I listen for when trying new phones.

I'm really excited to let these break in a bit (though they really don't need it) and do some tip tuning to tame the bass a bit to my liking. I'd rather EQ a bit of boom out than try to eq in some bass that is not there.

They do not need a lot of volume to sound good. (the Tenore need a bit of volume to sound their best

They are very comfortable to wear. Not too heavy, not too light and feel really balanced in the ear even though they stick out a bit. The shape makes them super easy to take in and out and the strain relief you can see in the picture means you don't have to be super careful of the cables.

I am super impressed with what I got for $22 dollars and plan to get a pair for myself at that price.
text_fidelity_b: Symphonized Wired Earbuds with Microphone - Noise Isolating Headphones with Wire, Ear Buds with Wire, Headphones with Microphone for Computer, Corded Earbuds, Travel Headphones 3.5mm Graduation Gift

The quality is good, but the set up is confusing and complicated. I thought that this would automatically download the clips to the app and I would chose which ones I wanted to keep or not (this is the way that my husbands does). The DWL-800AP+ will repeat the wireless signal of:

text_fidelity_a:
Audio-Technica ATH-LS50iSBK In-Ear Monitor Headphones with In-Line Mic & Control, Black Very good headphones. Smallish ear pieces and the black plastic shell is not real attractive, but they feel solid and well made. Rubber ear tips are comfortable for long periods of time and 3 different sizes of replacement tips are included. Bass is very good and overall sound clarity is much better than with cheap headphones. Full volume is more than loud enough for me and distortion at the highest volume is tolerable (unlike with cheap headphones). Wrap-around cables can be a hassle, but these have thicker wires and don't tangle as much as others that I have tried. Wrap-around cables really prevent the earbuds from falling out when I am working out. A simple nylon bag is the only carrying case included in the oversized box, but better cases are available at dollar stores.

Yes, Apple is trying to kill off wired headphones, but wired headphones still have huge advantages over Bluetooth, such as not having to worry about battery life, being able to recharge your phone at the same time you are listening to music, and of course the sound quality of wired headphones is usually better than similarly priced Bluetooth headphones.
text_fidelity_b: Audio-Technica ATH-LS50iSBK In-Ear Monitor Headphones with In-Line Mic & Control, Black

text_fidelity_a:
Corsair Vengeance 2000 Wireless 7.1 Gaming Headset (CA-9011115-NA) For the price, this is a decent set of gaming headphones. The build quality is perfectly fine for the price point. It doesn't feel as rock solid as more expensive brands, but feels like it will certainly stand up to normal usage.

The comfort is borderline. It feels fine for up to about an hour of usage, then the ear cups start to become somewhat uncomfortable and the headband pinches a bit. It's not the best set for hours and hours of usage, but for "normal" wear times I didn't have any problems.

The sound quality is quite good. Nice amount of bass response without sounding muddy. I also found it to have more than good enough sound quality for watching movies, with the dialogue coming through clearly. It's not the best for listening to music (the mid and upper ranges are a bit constrained) but for it's intended purpose of a gaming set, no complaints at all regarding sound quality.

My major problem was with range. I love the fact that these are wireless, but placement is critical. I'd lose the signal if I didn't vary much from a specific spot near the wireless adapter. Moving just a bit out of the "zone" killed the connection. That was a disappointment since, while I didn't expect to be able to roam around the house with them on, I did expect to be able to leave my chair and go a short distance without breaking the connection. No problems with signal strength when seated or within a few feet of the adapter, but hit and miss when moving more than a few feet away.

Other than the range issue, this is a pretty good value in a gaming headphone set.
text_fidelity_b: Corsair Vengeance 2000 Wireless 7.1 Gaming Headset (CA-9011115-NA)

I use these earphones for running. They are a bit tight when placed over ears, but at the same time they stay on very well. I found ear cushions quite soft and comfortable. I did find it difficult to locate "backwards/softer" button by feel while earphones are worn, but eventually got used to it.
Overall I think its a very nice "bang for the buck" product. Time will tell whether or not sweat will cause problems; so far it has not.

text_fidelity_a:
FDY MP3 Player, MP3 Player with Bluetooth5.0, 32GB Portable Music Player with FM Radio/Recorder, HiFi Lossless Sound Quality, 2.4Inch Touch Screen Mini MP3 Player for Running, Expandable 128GB TF When I opened the package containing this MP3 player, I was amazed at how small it is. But immediately became delighted at its perfectly small size. It is not the size of a small cellphone, but rather like what should have naturally occurred if an iPod shuffle mated with an iPod Nano. Perfect size and perfect function.

As the product description does not list or show the size of this MP3 player I list them here:

Length: 2 3/4 inches Width: 2 inches Thickness: 3/8 inch

Yes, small, but a powerhouse in functionality. I really miss the days when an MP3 player just played music. After a near fatal fall of my phone (luckily just the screen protector cracked!) it became important that an expensive phone might not be the best thing to lug around while performing yardwork. This excellent device solves that issue, and solves it well.

Songs and MP3 audio books were loaded easily onto the player. It is not made by Apple nor is part of their line, so the iTunes program does not work with this. However, it is a easy fix - just go to your Music folder on your computer, and drop the files you wish into this device's memory. Easy peasy and quick. It comes with an included 32 GB of memory, but can easily be upgraded if you install your own micro SD card, up to 128 GB.

It comes with wired earphones, which I did not use or test. With the invention of easy to pair Bluetooth earphones, I have no desire to be ever tethered with a headphone cord again. The player pairs easily with all 3 of my Bluetooth devices - earphones, headphones, and speakers. The sound from each device is flawless, which might be a function of the device, but is also determined by the source.

There are just 3 buttons on the side of this MP3 player - on/off button, volume up, and volume down. All other functions are controlled by the small but well designed touch screen. It is very comparable with the touch capability of modern phones, the programs are opened with ease and operate in an intuitive logical manner. There are other functions built into this device, but since I really got it as an MP3 player, that is what I am focused upon.

With this player comes a handy removable back clip, letting you clip it on/in a pocket, armband, belt, anywhere. Without the clip, it is small enough to easily slip into any pocked of your cloths, even the tiny change pockets in most jeans. Besides the wired earphones & clip, there is a 3mm audio cable for attaching it manually to another device, and a Micro USB cable for charging. There is a plastic protective film on the front face - it can be removed, but the touch screen operates just fine if it is left on.

This is my new favorite toy, It it not cheap or flimsy, but in all honesty, looks and feels like a tiny cell phone in how its constructed. It does not happen often, but this wonderful MP3 player exceeded my expectations.
text_fidelity_b: FDY MP3 Player, MP3 Player with Bluetooth5.0, 32GB Portable Music Player with FM Radio/Recorder, HiFi Lossless Sound Quality, 2.4Inch Touch Screen Mini MP3 Player for Running, Expandable 128GB TF

text_fidelity_a:
(OLD MODEL) Seagate Expansion 3TB Desktop External Hard Drive USB 3.0 (STBV3000100) So far, the hard drive is working as one would expect. As always with these things, the questions mostly arise in longevity/reliability issues, so I'll be updating this once I've had a longer time to determine how it does in those categories. First impressions at this point, though:

1) the drive has a relatively small footprint, which is nice

2) Feels quite sturdy and hefty (it's surprisingly heavy) with good build quality

3) This isn't powered by your USB, so you'll need an outlet for its enclosed power cord

4) When you start up, it takes a little while (a few seconds) for the display light to come on. At first, I thought it hadn't started up at all, but just wait a small bit and it will light up

5) the display light is located on top but at the rear of the device, which while minor, is a slight inconvenience. I have it under my desk set back a little ways, so to see the light isn't as immediate as one might like

6) the drive is quite quiet. Not silent--you can hear it--but definitely quieter than many I've had

7) the drive is pretty fast, with the uptick from USB 2 to 3 very noticeable as I move from one computer (USB 2) to the other (USB 3)--it varies depending on what I'm copying, but sometimes the difference is half the speed

8) despite the small footprint, with its necessity for power and it's weight, I wouldn't consider this at all a portable drive, though I suppose you could use it as such. But really, it's big and heavy for that.

9) I use this on several Macs--no problem at all reformatting it for those computers--just a few mouse clicks and a few seconds is all

So far, this is a good big backup drive (I have the 5 TB version). And since we all know, or should, that drives will fail, you can't have too many of them. If any issues arise over time, I'll update accordingly
text_fidelity_b: (OLD MODEL) Seagate Expansion 3TB Desktop External Hard Drive USB 3.0 (STBV3000100)

text_fidelity_a:
KZ ZS10 Pro, Linsoul 4BA+1DD 5 Driver in Ear Monitor, HiFi Metal Earphones, with Stainless Steel Faceplate, 2 Pin Detachable Cable (Without Mic, Black) Best sounding in-ear headphones I've ever heard, by a mile. I've owned the Bang and Olufsen H3, Sony XBA H1, Klipsch S4, X7, X6i, 1More Dual Drivers, Beats by Dr Dre Tour (wired), and Monster Cable's Jamz and Turbines.

The bass has lots of range and goes DEEP, in some tracks it even reminds me of my Kicker CVR 12' car subwoofer I used to blast about 15 years ago. It is not quite that overpowering, of course, and it balances out nicely with the other frequencies. The midrange is very present and natural sounding judging by how vocals and guitar strings sound. The highs are beautiful, they sound very accurate to me and present no sibilance. The overall sound is very rich and detailed, it allows you to follow specific instruments as you listen, and it even presents some soundstage (which I didn't think was possible in in-ears, maybe my aforementioned B&O H3 had some)

Overall these do have a V sound signature with boosted bass and treble, but not as marked as almost everything else that's in the market. In order to eliminate any fatigue caused by this, I would strongly recommend that you disable any bass boost, make sure you're not elevating bass or treble at all in EQ, and go even deeper and disable default features like Dolby Atmos (Oneplus phone) and even the Hi Fi quad DAC on LG phones (which I've found does introduce a bit of a V curve itself)

Other than their sound these earphones' build quality seems very good and durable. I'm in disbelief they could cost $60. You're welcome
text_fidelity_b: KZ ZS10 Pro, Linsoul 4BA+1DD 5 Driver in Ear Monitor, HiFi Metal Earphones, with Stainless Steel Faceplate, 2 Pin Detachable Cable (Without Mic, Black)

I'm definitely buying more - and hiding them from the teens.

I have a leather BookBook for my Air that I really like, but sometimes I want a case with a slimmer profile, and the Acme sleeve is perfect for those times.

I have the Grey/Poppy Orange sleeve, which I think is a nice combo. The Poppy Orange does look closer to red in my opinion.

The inside of the sleeve has a soft material, to protect against scratches, and each side has a reinforced plastic insert, to provide a little extra protection. The outside is made from neoprene, which should provide some protection from water. I wouldn’t say it makes your laptop waterproof, because water could sneak in the open top, but there’s some protection.

The elastic band isn’t actually necessary, since the sleeve is such a tight fit, but a) It looks spiffy and b) You could clip pens or slip something extra underneath it.

I do have a concern for the stitching on the sides and bottom, which doesn’t seem stretchy. Not that I plan to put more than my Air in here, but I worry that I could strain the stitching eventually. The stitching also takes away from the waterproofing of the case, since water could conceivably sneak in-between the gaps.

Fire HD 10 Tablet with Alexa, 10.1" HD Display, 16 GB, Black - with Special Offers (Previous Generation - 5th) Love it! Waited all year long to get this for Christmas. I have been owning an iPod (for music and video), a 7 inch Kindle (for books, music and video, and a laptop PC for email and everything else. Because of how much I like Amazon Prime Music and Music Unlimited, I decided to try to reduce the amount of high dollar items I need to replace every 3 to 4 years. So I am attempting to use the 10 inch Kindle to replace both the iPod and PC laptop.

So far so good. Email is easy to use. I have loaded the HP ePrint app to be able to print out bills I pay online, etc for records. Having the music available on any device is wonderful. I also have a 7 inch Kindle HDX my wife uses and access the music on my Android Smartphone as well.

The Kindle HD 10 has a wonderful picture. Nice to be able to use the Xfinity app to watch shows off my DVR, like Atlanta Hawks games while my wife watches something else on the large tv. Much better than watching on my 5 inch smartphone screen.

The audio is good and if I want to play it louder can send it over to one of my bluetooth speakers. I use the bluetooth keyboard and love it. That is what allows me to replace my PC as I can type emails rather than one finger type them.

I got the 16 GB with 128 GB SD memory card. Adding the memory card slot is a big improvement over previous kindles I have.

I read graphic novels like The Walking Dead series and being able to see them easily on the 10 inch screen is also a big improvement.

I highly recommend this!

text_fidelity_a:
ViewSonic 32 Inch 1080p Widescreen IPS Monitor with Ultra-Thin Bezels, Screen Split Capability HDMI and DisplayPort (VX3276-MHD) Caveat: for gaming, this is four stars. Its refresh rate is nothing noteworthy, and it lacks any kind of sync technology. My son and I swapped it in for each of his G-Sync monitors, and he said someone who'd never had G-Sync would probably like it a lot. Then, he took his own monitors back.

HOWEVER, when I took it to my husband's recording studio to test on Pro Tools, I almost had to fight him to get it back.

The QHD, blue screen filter, and other features make this perfect for anyone who is working long hours at anything that needs decent responsiveness and excellent resolution (film or photo editing, music production). The refresh rate is plenty good for Pro Tools, and the monitor is the best we've used so far at reducing fatigue.

Bottom Line: my son is keeping his G-Syncs, but my husband will be trying to wrestle me for the Viewsonic. I plan on keeping it in the home office, where he does some of his mixing and I watch streaming video. But he really wants to take it to his studio. And based on our field test of it there, that's where it really shines. So, we might be getting another one in the near future.
text_fidelity_b: ViewSonic 32 Inch 1080p Widescreen IPS Monitor with Ultra-Thin Bezels, Screen Split Capability HDMI and DisplayPort (VX3276-MHD)

Samsung Gear Fit2 Smartwatch Large, Black After struggling with an early incarnation of a Fitbit, this watch is a breeze. I honestly do not understand the negative reviews, unless a few lemons were sent out.

It couldn't be easier, because the app explains everything and walks you through the process. It's well thought-out and intuitive.
And while the primary goal is as a fitness watch, which it excels at, I really get a kick out of the fact that I can get all my push notifications on it, and even read emails and texts on it.
But back to Fitness. Of course, it acts as a pedometer. But it also measures your heartbeat, every 5 minutes. This thing keeps track of everything! It even knows what kind of exercise you're doing. It maps out progress so that it's easier to keep an eye on where your goals are and how to meet them.

Tripp Lite 550VA UPS Battery Backup, 300W Eco Green, USB, RJ11, 8 Outlets (ECO550UPS), Black Like everyone in California, we've been having a lot of power outages and spotty power, and through that, I've been really made aware how important it is to have steady, continuous power to my devices and not be affected by brownouts or power surges. I also really appreciate that when the power goes out suddenly, I have enough time to save my work, print a document, or do any last critical wrap up before things go dark. This battery backup has been great!

If you have used battery backup in the past you generally know what to expect, you plug it into the wall, plug in your devices, and when the power goes out you have a little bit of time, depending on which devices are sapping power from it and how much juice they take, to finish up what you are doing and shut down properly.

What is interesting to me about this one is that it has something that automatically powers down accessory devices like your monitor or scanner when the master device is off. So I have the one plug for the master device, which is my computer, and one plug that is on battery backup that will power down and accessory device like my monitor when my computer is not on, and three plugs that will power down accessory devices and not have them on battery backup, good for things like my scanner. While I haven't hooked up a power reader to determine exactly my savings, I do know for sure that some of these accessory devices are indeed using power when they are not being used, so I really appreciate the thoughtfulness of this.

There are also some regular plugs, some of which are battery backup and some not. This is perfect because there are ample plugs for everything and I can really set things up just the way I need so that my printer is not drawing battery power during a power outage unless I actually want it to.

It's working as expected and seems to be designed with care. I definitely recommend this.

text_fidelity_a:
Fitbit Sense 2 Advanced Health and Fitness Smartwatch with Tools to Manage Stress and Sleep, ECG App, SpO2, 24/7 Heart Rate and GPS, Shadow Grey/Graphite, One Size (S & L Bands Included) At this point, I have had the Sense 2 for 2 days and I know at least some of my issues will likely be fixed with later software updates. First, the good. I like the form factor. The case is thin and the watch, even with the supplied band, is comfortable. Speaking of the band, as a big guy, I was overjoyed to see the inclusion of a second band that actually fit. Also, changing bands is a snap.

Overall, it seems to be relatively high quality. The battery life, so far at least has been fantastic. I am on hour 42 of wearing it after a 99% charge and it is down to 70% battery left. The screen is fairly bright and crisp. An understated advantage of the Sense 2 (and one of the reasons I switched) is that is OS and phone brand agnostic. You can use it with Apple or Android and, unlike the Galaxy Watch, there are no features locked away if you are not using the correct brand of phone.

If you are coming from a Galaxy Watch where you could customize the watch face and all sorts of other things and that is important to you, then move along. This watch will not be for you. For now, at least, there is not really much substantive you can do to individualize your user experience. That's not so great.

Also not so great is the things that are missing. There is no Google Maps at launch. Also, despite being a Google company, no support for the Google Assistant (Alexa only sadly). There is also no interface to control music on your phone if that is important to you. I found it mildly annoying, but not a deal breaker. In addition, some people will be turned off by the fact that there are features that require a Fitbit paid subscription to get, even though you get six months for free.

The real reason I bought this watch was the ECG function. I have had A Fib for a couple of years and used to use (and still do) a Kardia XL to check my rhythm. The Galaxy Watch 4 was nice because it did a reasonable single lead reading and it meant not having to carry another gizmo with me. You simply held still and put a finger on each of the side buttons. Unfortunately, when I switched from a Galaxy phone to a Pixel, I lost the ability to do an ECG.

On the Sense 2, the ECG has not been impressive. First, I have big hands and contorting my right one to get my thumb and forefinger on the corner of the glass has been a challenge at time. It often takes several tries to get it right. Second, despite confirming on both my Kardia and my Galaxy Watch, the Sense 2 will never indicate that I am in A Fib. Apparently, if your pulse goes above 120 (which mine frequently does while in A Fib) then the Sense 2 just gives up and won't really check. Even in instances where it was below 120, the Sense will not confirm. I guess we get to settle for inconclusive results instead. Given this feature was the main reason I bought the watch, it may be a deal breaker for me and I may return it for that reason. If this feature is not that important to you, then it may still be a good option.

Overall though, it may be a good option for the right person. If you care primarily about health and fitness tracking and want a good battery life, then this is a good option. At the current $300 price point, I still feel like Fitbit may be asking a little too much given the features of the other higher end options on the market.
text_fidelity_b: Fitbit Sense 2 Advanced Health and Fitness Smartwatch with Tools to Manage Stress and Sleep, ECG App, SpO2, 24/7 Heart Rate and GPS, Shadow Grey/Graphite, One Size (S & L Bands Included)

Amazon Basics Single Monitor Stand, Lift Engine Arm Mount, Black At the time of this review, there is not a regular Amazon page on this product, but it appears to conform to VESA sizing D, with both 75mm and 100mm square hole patterns. Manual says it is rated up to 25 lbs.

When mounted properly, this thing is extremely sturdy, professional looking, and versatile. You will be able to adjust your monitor or TV in any way you can imagine, including fixed or dynamic switching from landscape to portrait. To mount properly, you do need a stud if mounting to an interior wall. They also supply anchors for masonry mounting.

The top cover for the wall plate says Amazon Basics, which actually makes it look less generic, although I am sure some people don't want any extra color or logos on their walls. You can leave this off, but then the hardware will show (in black). The upper arm also has a discreet logo. It has a medium flat black finish that looks high end (as usual, I think Amazon's stuff looks better than "basic" does justice).

Both arms are approximately 10" from pivot point to pivot point, so you can get at least a 20" reach in any direction, or sit the monitor pretty much flat against the wall without any hardware showing.

The lower arm has a roomy chamber for cables that can probably hold 8 RG-6 sized cables, or at least four larger cables. Unfortunately, the upper arm has no room for cables, so you can only do as good as using the included black tie wraps to keep them in place. If all your cables are black, it won't be much of an eyesore.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Basics Single Monitor Stand, Lift Engine Arm Mount, Black

text_fidelity_a:
Fire HD 10 Tablet with Alexa Hands-Free, 10.1" 1080p Full HD Display, 32 GB, Marine Blue (Previous Generation - 7th) I'm not going to delve into the technical aspects of the Fire as others have done an admirable job already. But as an alternative to other, more expensive tablets, the Fire is an amazing piece of tech.

I was almost getting ready to pull the trigger on the Google Pixel C or Samsung S3. A big leap for me as I didn't want to spend $500 plus on a tablet, but I wanted fast speed, large screen, and inexpensive aftermarket accessories.

The Fire is dual-core, so it flies through the games I play. A big plus. I know everyone hates when their game bogs down in the middle of a rousing Orc battle, or, even worse, won't even load. The Fire has run all the games I've thrown at it with no issues.

The 10" screen is heavenly, considering I came from a generic 7" tablet that was VGA on a good day. The text is crisp, the graphics flow as they should. HD movies and shows are freakin' excellent. The 10" format seems to be the best for this.

If you research well for accessories, you can find some nice deals. There was no way I was going to spring for a $30 case, when the $10 Fintie case works as good or better. More money saved for movies, games, and books!

Please don't spend the extra $15 on the 'without special offers' option. The only special offers thrown at you are when the tablet wakes from sleep. A quick swipe and they're gone. Save that money for a case!

And yes, Virginia, you can get the google play store. The easiest way is to install 4 app files and run them in order. No rooting, no PC hookups. Go to blog.ebook-reader dot com and search 'how to install google play on fire.' Easy peasy, just follow the instructions to the letter.

All-in-all this a capable tablet offered by Amazon. The price is right, the tech is excellent considering its price point. You can game like a madman, watch shows, and read War & Peace.
text_fidelity_b: Fire HD 10 Tablet with Alexa Hands-Free, 10.1" 1080p Full HD Display, 32 GB, Marine Blue (Previous Generation - 7th)

Jabra Talk 65 Mono - Premium Wireless Single Ear Headset - 2 Built-in Noise Cancelling Microphones, Media Streaming, Up to 100 Meters Bluetooth Range - Black Jabra Talk 45 Bluetooth Earpiece has many features that will satisfy users needs as listed below:

Battery life: for me was around 10 hours of life, recharge time was also quick at around 90 minutes to fully recharge. Not bad for a Bluetooth earpiece.

Sound quality: Sound quality was surprisingly high for such a small unit, clear and without any distortion or hiss some other units I have used had. Volume adjustment also provided a good range for most circumstances.

Comfort: This is where most Bluetooth earpieces fail me, because they are just too uncomfortable to wear for any period of time. The Jabra Talk 45 is lightweight and comfortable for extended wear. The two earpiece rings are sized for different people, not just a single sized loop. Put the correct size loop on and you should be good to go. My only ding on this is the earpiece loops are a little flimsy for daily extended use.

Connectivity: The Jabra Talk 45 connected to my phone right away, no issue there. I did have an issue connecting it to my laptop for a Skype call. It would just never be recognized by my laptop to make the Skype call, this is my only real complaint with the Jabra Talk 45.

Creative Zen X-Fi 8 GB Video MP3 Player with Built-In Speaker (Black/Silver) Zen X-Fi 16GB review 2-28-09

Had the Zen X-Fi 16GB for two months of daily use now.

The device is well built and solid. It needs a silicon skin for protection, though. That is extra but highly recommended so your expensive player doesn't slip out of your pocket.

First, the buttons are too flat and are not illuminated. Sounds like a small thing, but flat black metal buttons against a black metal background in the car at night are very difficult to find and press. If the buttons were transparent and had the tiniest LED behind them, they would be a lot easier to manipulate accurately.

No Bluetooth--I'm getting very tired of wired connection to my car and headphones. LOSE THE WIRES, Creative! The earphones that come with the Zen are terrific. Really good quality. But the wires are tiresome.

Though I'd rather have Bluetooth, Zen is Wi-Fi capable. You can wirelessly hook to your computer's wireless router and play or copy files back and forth, but it's so frustrating to make it function it's virtually useless. USB cable is the way to connect.

As part of Wi-Fi, Creative does provide something called "Media Server" that you can access via your internet connection wireless router if you're in range and properly connected. After waiting a couple of minutes for the connection to be made, you can listen to propaganda from all kinds of politically correct content like NPR, the BBC, Australia's ABC and KCRW. Yes, master: I hear and obey. Mostly a waste as you can't really select content you want, only what they supply. Definitely politically correct. And boring.

It has a kind of chat texting capability but that's what phones are for these days and the Zen's dinky keyboard just doesn't cut it. The keyboard is laid out the way it is so it can emulate a phone keypad when you're in chat mode. Too frustrating to use. It's why QWERTY keyboards are on phones now.

Bookmarks. A few minutes after being shut off, the Zen forgets where you were when you shut down. If you fire it up an hour after shutdown or dock it to your computer to upload new content, it starts playing the last file you opened from the beginning. This is a bit frustrating when you're part way through a three hour podcast. So Creative allows you to set a Bookmark from within the file you are playing. It's quick and easy once you figure it out. I use it all the time now. This allows you to set a point in a podcast so you can return to it later. But while you can set the bookmark from within the file, you have to navigate to the Bookmarks screen to select the bookmark when playing back later. Not very intuitive. Took me two months to realize the usefulness of the feature. Why doesn't it simply remember where I stopped listening by itself? My DVR does. Just resume from where I left off. But no.

The lower left button is programmable. It's called My Shortcut. You pick from a list of available functions and set it. This allows you to go to a particular favorite screen or function once you decide what that is.

The Zen first and foremost is marketed as a video and MP3 player. What I wish it could do is have a "skip forward" ability (again, like my DVR does) that allows me to skip forward 30 seconds or a minute (or a user defined amount) so I can move forward in predictable amounts instead of holding the fast forward button down. If it's going to be called a "player" of any sort, it should have a variety of player controls. Skip forward/back should be available. Firmware upgrade wish, Creative.

Speaking of the fast forward button, the longer you hold it, the faster it goes. It starts by forwarding at a slow rate, then speeds up until you are jumping forward minutes at a time. This is good for zooming to a point quickly. But if you want to go forward, say, seven minutes, holding the FFwd button down too long will launch it into hyperdrive and you'll be at 10 minutes or more into the file, then have to rewind/search back. Somewhat of a pain. No. A real pain. Let me skip forward or back in 30 second increments.

A great feature is its built-in speaker. It sounds like my transistor radio from my childhood. This feature was the main reason I bought the Zen: you don't have to use earphones if you don't want to. It is a great and rare feature among MP3 players. A pocketable mini boombox.

Creative's Centrale "iTunes wannabe" software is dreadful. I tried it for awhile, then uninstalled it and now just drag files to the device.

Video screen quality is very good but 320x240 is still a bit small. Diagonally it's 2-1/2"; 2" wide x 1-5/8" high. It's also the old 4:3 aspect ratio, not the modern 16:9. If you're viewing a 16:9 video letterboxed, you are looking at one tiny video.

The video player (as opposed to the music player) is very weak. Windows Media Player 11 it ain't. Another key reason I bought the Zen is because it promised it could play a plethora of video formats. Wrong. I have dozens of wmv video files which exist in many sizes and bitrates from thumbnails to HD. Unfortunately, almost all of them need to be converted via Creative's stand-alone converter app or Centrale into squeezed-down bitrates and 320x240 size. This process is clumsy and slow.

If virtually every file needs to be converted in order to play, it's not really playing the advertised list of formats: it's playing the format Creative has selected and must be converted to. Often, even if I render out a wmv directly from my video editing software to Creative's parameters, it still won't play properly without conversion. Yet another marketing promise dashed to pieces.

The Zen allows me to delete files directly from the Zen if I want to (as opposed to needing to plug into iTunes to delete or add). This is good.

It has a built in mic and audio recording capability and you can program the "My Shortcut" button to start the recording process immediately so you don't have to navigate to the recorder's controls.

It has an FM radio that only works if the ear phones are plugged in because the wire becomes the antenna. What I'd really like is an AM radio, though, for news, talk radio, traffic and weather. Who needs FM? That's what your MP3's are for in the first place, right?

The unit has an SD card slot, but it's not well integrated. Content on the SD card does not appear in the normal file list. You must navigate to the card and browse it separately. Worse, when you do that, it comes back with "There are no playable files in this folder" even when I know I put mp3 files on the card that the player can play. You have to use the "Import" function to move files from the SD card to the player's memory in order to play them. Think of the SD card as an aux thumb drive, not as expanded memory, except it doesn't even work like that, actually. If you think you can buy the 16GB and "double" its memory capacity with a card, think again. It's more of a gimmick than a useful feature. More Creative fluff that is long on promise but short on delivery.

By the way, when you plug the Zen into your computer's USB cable the Zen does not mount as a drive (what Windows calls a "Local Disk.") It "docks" as a "Portable Media Player" according to Type in Windows Explorer. This means you can't play directly from the player. If you click on a file on the Zen from within Windows, it moves the file to a temp folder on your C: drive before playing. Not a big deal, but if you intend on connecting the Zen to a USB input on your car stereo or computer, I don't think your stereo will be able to see the Zen's contents. While the Zen is docked to the computer, all the play buttons are disabled and the display indicates "Docked" until you unplug the device. On the other hand, you don't have to unmount the device. Just pull from the USB and go.

Poor Creative. Always trying. Never quite getting there. Won't be long now and a phone will do it all. Look at Sony Erickson's W760, iPhone or Palm Pre.
text_fidelity_b: Creative Zen X-Fi 8 GB Video MP3 Player with Built-In Speaker (Black/Silver)

text_fidelity_a:
POWAITER Power Strip with USB C, 3 Outlets & 2 USB Ports (18W USB C) Desktop Charging Station,Flat Plug and 5 ft Long Extension Cords, Compact Size and Lightweight for Travel,Home and Office,White This is pretty great in some ways. I love the flat plug, the plain white to blend in with painted baseboards, the overall compact size, and having one of each type of USB port. I keep mine under the couch so I can slide it out if I need to plug stuff in temporarily, which I often do from that location.

It sort of annoys me that an LED is on whenever this is plugged in. I know most chargers don't draw a whole lot of vampire energy, but I'd allow myself to be convinced of that further if it didn't have a light on all the time. Since I don't really use it in my situation all that often, I wonder if I should just go back to two individual extension cords (but this is more versatile).

Also, although it could sometimes get in the way if you didn't want it, I think all power strips should have a power switch. In that case, the light would be useful. I like to cut power to a lot of things when not in use (especially electronics, and even more so supposedly "smart" devices that just stay connected to the Internet all the time needlessly.

Great format, but wishing for a power switch.
text_fidelity_b: POWAITER Power Strip with USB C, 3 Outlets & 2 USB Ports (18W USB C) Desktop Charging Station,Flat Plug and 5 ft Long Extension Cords, Compact Size and Lightweight for Travel,Home and Office,White
